title: INC-401 · C2 Building Shared AP Capacity
summary: Six third-floor labs share one assumed 100 Mbps access point; the 120 Mbps aggregate is mathematically consistent but underdetermined.
description: On the 3rd floor of C2 Building, Labs 1–6 share a single access point with an assumed capacity of 100 Mbps. Pairwise readings give x₁ + x₂ = 35, x₃ + x₄ = 40 and x₅ + x₆ = 45 Mbps, while the observed aggregate demand is 120 Mbps. The fourth equation is the sum of the first three, so the model is consistent but rank-deficient: it cannot identify an individual lab's demand.
investigationSteps: Assign one unknown x₁…x₆ to each lab's demand on the shared AP, in Mbps.
Convert the three pairwise readings and the aggregate reading into four equations.
Reduce the augmented matrix and inspect rank, pivot columns and free parameters.
Compare the aggregate demand with the assumed AP capacity separately from the algebra.

capacity.note: Capacity comparison is a planning observation, not a row of the linear system. It does not prove a physical network fault.

templateFindings: The fourth equation is exactly the sum of the first three, so it adds no independent constraint. RREF has rank 3 for 6 unknowns and three free parameters, giving infinitely many valid lab-by-lab splits.
Consistency means the four readings agree algebraically. It does not identify any individual lab demand and does not prove that the access point is faulty.
Separately from the algebra, 120 Mbps observed aggregate demand exceeds the assumed 100 Mbps AP capacity by 20 Mbps. That is a capacity-planning observation, not a mathematical contradiction.
suggestedActions: Verify the 100 Mbps rating in the asset register before treating the 20 Mbps excess as confirmed.
Add independent per-lab measurements, such as a difference sensor, to identify individual x₁…x₆ values.
Re-run the model with those measurements and review AP placement or load balancing if the excess persists.
